Frames 1 and 4 are symmetric, centred layouts that feel like parameter sweeps; composition should be pushed as hard as in frames 3 and 5

tells: Photogrammetry and point-cloud capture of real streets, deliberately broken: the data is corrupted and the geometry spikes. The medium is the subject.
Real texture and depth. Scanned brick, sky and fire skies give material richness.

tells: Generative Voronoi tessellation driven by a source (a face or a figure). The cell density follows image luminance, which shows a working, considered system.

The frames change real structure (radial clusters, horizontal bands, a rectangle frame, a face), so the sequence implies evolving parameters.

No type. Its absence suits an abstract audiovisual piece, but nothing makes up for it.
gaps: Voronoi-on-image is a stock creative-coding technique. It needs a distinctive idea or an emotional arc to stand above the generative genre.
Grey gradients with flat lighting have no material, colour or light idea. Rendering the cells as a physical substance or using a deliberate palette would help.
Composition is often centre-weighted and similar across frames. It needs bolder framing and more scale contrast.

tells: A Voronoi tessellation is the whole visual language, and it is built up rather than applied as a filter: cell density is used to sculpt form, with fine cells resolving a face and coarse cells as void.

There is clear choreography across the frames: an open symmetrical field, then horizontal striations on an inverted white ground, then a figure in profile, then a rectangular frame-within-frame, then a frontal face reveal. Each state is different.
The figure emerges out of abstraction, which is the payoff a structure-then-reveal music video needs.
The palette is strictly monochrome. That is a choice, though it is safe. No type is visible, and the abstraction is better without it.
The risk is that it reads as a well-art-directed Processing/TouchDesigner sketch. The flat grey vignettes in frames 1 and 4 are close to a default look.
gaps: It has no material or light beyond line-on-gradient. Giving the cells depth, glow or a photographic source plate would add the tactile richness C has.
The palette is pure greyscale. One deliberate chromatic event, for example at the face reveal, would make the climax land.
The generative technique is still close to the idea itself. It needs a clearer conceptual reason why this subject breaks into Voronoi cells, so the piece isn't just a demo of the algorithm.

tells: It uses photogrammetry and point-cloud material, broken intentionally: corrupted scans of red-brick streets, an extruded spiky landscape, a tiny-planet ring of houses against a fire sky, and a wireframe corridor overlaid with code and text.
There is real variety and camera travel between frames, implying flythroughs, inversions and a clear arc from inside the scan to outside it.
The typed fragments ('midi', 'theory', 'point cloud') look like considered monospace annotation rather than titles, which suits the data-glitch theme.

But the colour is muddy in places (frames 2 and 5), and the corruption looks partly like uncontrolled artefacts rather than designed decay. It sits closer to an artist experiment or VJ loop than a polished studio film.
gaps: Control the glitch. Each corruption should be designed and readable, not noise, with a consistent grade and palette instead of saturated red mixed with grey sky and pink rock.
Composition needs focal hierarchy. Several frames are uniformly busy with no point where the eye rests.
The text layer should be typographically shaped, with scale, rhythm and placement in space, so it reads as a designed system rather than scattered terminal output.

Push the human subject further: the face reveal is strong, but the middle frames lean on the algorithm and lack narrative

defects: No busy-moment strips were provided, so motion can only be judged from pairs and samples. In those, the lights come on letter by letter in place ('LOW' → 'LOW TIDE') with no visible spacing, overshoot or camera response.
In two of the three pairs, the 1/6 s frames are nearly identical: the type sits static over a slow water plate for several seconds, so there is a lot of dead air.
The opening frame is mostly an empty dark sea with a thin row of dots. It is a weak first image and wastes about 3 s, which matches the measured per-second change of 3.7 to 3.8.
The harbour shots have low contrast: blue-grey lights on navy at a modest level that will block up on most displays, and the horizon band of reflections is muddy and hard to read.
The partial light-out state ('WHEN THE LIGHTS', with letters missing) reads more like a render glitch than a designed decay. The scattered dots have no structure.

At 100%, the dot grid shows faint uneven brightness and a few stray red-orange dots outside the glyphs. The bloom is gentle but flat: there is no lens character and no depth-of-field variation between the near and far layers.
The water plate has a soft, slightly smeared look (it may be synthetic), which sits poorly against the crisp dot grid.
gaps: The motion needs to be built. The light-type device is good, but it only switches on and off in place. Top work would choreograph the lights: letters rippling on with offset timing, flickering, swaying with the tide, the camera drifting or racking focus, and lights migrating between lines as a handoff instead of a hard swap at the cut.

Picture and music need to lock together. The track has a clear dropout around 16.0 s and a bright full-band hit at about 17.3 s, but in the samples only a colour change (cool to warm 'ON') answers it. The phrase landings and the earlier section change around 7.3 s are not visibly mirrored by light hits, camera moves or cuts.

The film needs more range across shots and stronger frames. Every shot is the same flat, front-on text card over dark water at the same scale and depth. The piece needs a wide-to-close progression, real lights interacting with the reflection, and a stronger opening image that the warm 'ON' ending could rhyme with.
